title: Beatrix and the Puddle Chart
markdown:
The trees remember this story well, as do the busy little streams that tumble through the meadows. Whoooo, it was a time of rain, a drumming, happy rain that made the whole world shine like a jewel.

Now, in a snug little school nestled beside the twisty, whispering river, lived Beatrix. Beatrix was an otter. She had sleek, dark fur that was very good at staying waterproof, and paws that were quick and good at doing otter things. Her most important thing, especially after a good, thorough rain, was puddles. Oh, how Beatrix loved puddles! She loved their cool, still tops that showed the sky like shiny glass, their fun splashes when you stepped in them with a happy *sploosh*, and the way they held little secrets, like fallen, rust-coloured leaves or the quick zig-zagging of water striders. So, when the sunbeams finally peeked through the clouds after a very wet day, Beatrix had an idea.

“I know!” she chirped, her whiskers twitching with an excitement that made her whole body wiggle. “I shall make a Puddle Chart!”

Her friend, Ollie the gull, was always happy and ready for a chat. He swooped down from the sky, his white wings a bright flash against the wet branches. "A chart for puddles, Beatrix? What a funny idea! Will it fly, like me?" he squawked, tilting his head with a curious tilt.

"Oh, Ollie," Beatrix giggled. She unrolled a big piece of smooth, pale bark she’d found near the river. "It's to measure them. See? I’ll mark down each puddle, how wide it is, how deep. A proper record for our school!” She imagined lines and numbers, neat and tidy, just how she liked things.

Headteacher Moss, a wise old badger, ambled over. His spectacles always sat just right on his nose, and he wore a soft moss waistcoat. His steps were slow and thoughtful, like the quiet turning of the seasons. "A Puddle Chart, Beatrix? That sounds like a very thoughtful project indeed," he said softly. He paused, his brow furrowed gently, not in a grumpy way, but in a thinking way. "But what is it you hope to learn from measuring puddles, little one?"

Beatrix paused, her eager whiskers still. This was a good question. It was a question that made her think, like a little pebble dropped into the quiet water of her mind. "Well," she began, trying to find the right words, "to know which is the biggest. And the deepest. The most… well, the most puddle-y!” She felt a little unsure. Was "puddle-y" a real thing?

Headteacher Moss smiled, a warm, crinkly smile that reached his wise old eyes. "Indeed. Patience now. All will be revealed in time." He patted her head gently with a soft paw.

And so, the very next day, the Puddle Chart was hung near the main entrance of the school, a place for everyone to see. Beatrix, with her trusty measuring twig that was just the right length, set to work. The playground, still damp and sparkling, had many little pools. There was the Wide Wanderer, a big puddle near the sturdy old oak tree, stretching out like a sleepy giant. And the Deep Digger, a surprisingly dark spot by the bicycle racks, which looked as if it might have secrets at its very bottom. Beatrix carefully measured and marked, her tongue poking out slightly with focus.

But then, things started to get interesting. Little Pip the dormouse, his nose twitching faster than a speedy bug, added a tiny, detailed drawing next to a small, sun-dappled puddle. Below it, in wobbly letters, he’d written, "This one’s cheerful! It sparkles like happy thoughts!"

Fern the fox, usually quite quiet, her movements as graceful as falling leaves, scribbled next to a puddle that sat at the base of a tall, proud poppy. "The Shimmering Secret is brave. It didn't run away from the wind, even though it's small."

Beatrix blinked. Brave? Shy? But… she was measuring their size! Her twig didn't have a "brave" setting. She felt a tiny flutter of confusion, like a little moth bumping against a window.

Ollie, who had been watching from his perch on the school roof, swooped down, landing with a little hop. "Ah, Beatrix! You see," he announced with great importance, "some puddles have a special sparkle, a certain *je ne sais quoi*! This one," he pointed with a wing to a puddle shaped like a perfect, tiny teacup, nestled between two smooth pebbles, "this one has grace. It's a Puddle of Poise! It holds the sky so nicely, don't you think?"

Beatrix felt a strange flutter, not quite of confusion anymore, but of a growing wonder. Her chart was becoming much more than just numbers and measurements. Other pupils added their own ideas, their own special ways of seeing. There was the Giggle Puddle, because it seemed to bubble and burble merrily whenever the sparrows splashed in it, sending tiny sprays into the air. And the Shy Shadow, tucked away under the broad leaves of a rhubarb plant, that only appeared when the sun was just right, peeking out shyly.

The Puddle Chart became the most liked spot in the whole school. Children gathered around it, not just to see which puddles were the biggest or the deepest, but to read about their interesting personalities. They would point and talk, their voices full of delight. Beatrix, however, started to notice something else. Some of the smaller, quieter puddles, the ones with the most delicate reflections and the gentlest shimmer, were being overlooked. They weren't as big as the Wide Wanderer, or as interesting as the Deep Digger.

One afternoon, she heard two older otters talking near the chart. "This chart’s a bit silly, really," one said, flicking his tail. "Only the really big ones are worth looking at. These little ones are just… wet spots. Nothing special."

Beatrix's heart felt like a heavy stone. She shivered, though it wasn't cold. This is fear, she realised. Her chart, meant to celebrate puddles, was making some seem not important, even to be gotten rid of. The cheerful chatter of the playground suddenly seemed far away, quiet as if she were underwater. The thought of the Shimmering Secret vanishing, of its delicate rainbow colours disappearing forever, felt like a sudden, cold splash right in her face.

Just as a groundskeeper, holding a large, metal shovel, was about to fill in the little puddle, Beatrix scurried forward, her paws flying over the damp ground. Ollie, his sharp eyes having seen what was happening, trailed closely behind, flapping his wings in worry. "Wait! Please, wait!" Beatrix cried, her voice a little shaky, but firm.

The groundskeeper stopped, his shovel ready. "What is it, Beatrix? What's the matter?"

"This puddle," she said, pointing with a trembling paw. "It's not just a wet spot. It’s… it’s a Puddle of Poetry! It shows the sky like a tiny, perfect mirror, and it has the colours of a rainbow, right here!" She pointed to the colourful sheen on the water's surface. The groundskeeper's rough boots crunched on the damp earth, the metal shovel glinted in the sun, and a faint, earthy smell rose from the disturbed soil.

Ollie nodded vigorously, bobbing his head. "Indeed! It has great character! Far more than that rather bouncy splash near the swings, if I may say so! That one is all flash and no finesse."

Headteacher Moss, drawn by the noise and the urgency in Beatrix’s voice, arrived, his badger footsteps soft on the grass. He looked at Beatrix, her fur ruffled with worry, then at the small, shimmering puddle, and then at the Puddle Chart, which was now covered not just in measurements, but in lots of drawings and enthusiastic descriptions.

"Ah, Beatrix," he said softly, his voice full of understanding. "It seems your chart has taught us something more important than size. It has taught us about liking things for what they are." He turned to the groundskeeper, a gentle smile on his face. "Perhaps, instead of filling it, we could appreciate this little wonder for what it is?" He then turned to the children who had gathered, their faces full of worry and curiosity. "Beatrix has shown us that every puddle, big or small, has its own special story. Some are big and wide, like open arms. Others are quiet and shimmering, like whispered secrets. Let us add a new part to our chart. A part for Puddle Personalities!"

A ripple of excitement went through the children. They eagerly began to draw and write about the special things about the puddles they loved, from the "Bold Boggy Basin" that made the biggest splashes, to the "Whispering Water Droplet" that seemed to hold the sound of the rain. The groundskeeper, a twinkle appearing in his eye, put his shovel away and found a small, smooth, grey stone. He carefully placed it beside the Shimmering Secret, a quiet marker of its specialness.

And so, the Puddle Chart became a place of true appreciation, a celebration of all that puddles could be. Beatrix, no longer just measuring with her twig, learned to see with her heart, with her friend Ollie always reminding her to look for the sparkle, the grace, and the quiet bravery in every small, watery wonder. Headteacher Moss smiled, watching them, knowing that sometimes, the most important lessons are found not in numbers, but in the wonderful, varied characters of the world around us. Whoooo could have guessed that a simple chart of puddles could teach them all so much about looking closer?
characters: Beatrix the otter, Ollie the gull, Headteacher Moss
